source_evidence.anchor: Remark 2.7.9 (MGF near the origin), from its opening through the displayed Taylor chain and the words 'as lambda tends to 0'
source_evidence.observation: The remark assumes a general random variable X has mean zero and unit variance, additionally assumes X bounded for simplicity, and informally writes E exp(lambda X) approximately equal to E[1 + lambda X + lambda^2 X^2/2 + o(lambda^2 X^2)] = 1 + lambda^2/2 approximately equal to exp(lambda^2/2) as lambda tends to zero. Both comparison symbols are approximation symbols, not equality signs.

source_evidence.anchor: Remark 2.7.9 continuation, from 'becomes an equality' through the Exp(1) sentence
source_evidence.observation: The remark says the approximation becomes equality for N(0,1), attributes the global and local quadratic MGF-bound characterizations to Propositions 2.5.2 and 2.7.1 respectively, and states that for X distributed as Exp(1) the MGF is infinite for lambda at least one.

source_evidence.anchor: Equation (2.12), 'a classical formula gives the moment generating function of X distributed as N(0,1)'
source_evidence.observation: For X distributed as N(0,1), E exp(lambda X) = exp(lambda^2/2) for every real lambda. This is an exact equality with a global real domain.

For a random variable X, the four tail, moment, square-MGF, and square-exponential-integrability properties are equivalent up to absolute constant factors. If E X = 0, they are also equivalent to existence of K5 > 0 such that E exp(lambda X) <= exp(K5^2 lambda^2) for all real lambda.

For a random variable X, the four exponential-tail, linear-moment-growth, absolute-value-MGF, and absolute exponential-integrability properties are equivalent up to absolute constant factors. If E X = 0, they are also equivalent to existence of K5 > 0 such that E exp(lambda X) <= exp(K5^2 lambda^2) whenever |lambda| <= 1/K5.

source_evidence.anchor: Example 2.7.8, definition of the exponential distribution and the specialization used immediately before Remark 2.7.9
source_evidence.observation: The source defines X distributed as Exp(r) for rate r > 0 as nonnegative with P{X >= t} = exp(-r t) for t >= 0; Remark 2.7.9 specializes this to rate one when asserting MGF divergence.

For the sub-exponential MGF characterization, X is centered (E X = 0); the underlying equivalent properties are Proposition 2.7.1(a)-(d). [Source: PDF page 21, printed page 32; anchor: 'Moreover, if E X = 0' and property (e).]

For the divergence example, X is a nonnegative rate-one exponential random variable, i.e. X is distributed as Exp(1). [Source: PDF page 23, printed page 34, Example 2.7.8 exponential-tail definition; PDF page 24, printed page 35, final sentence of Remark 2.7.9.]
conclusions: Informal local Taylor clause: as lambda tends to 0, the source writes E exp(lambda X) approximately equal to E[1 + lambda X + lambda^2 X^2/2 + o(lambda^2 X^2)] = 1 + lambda^2/2 approximately equal to exp(lambda^2/2). This displayed claim uses two informal approximation symbols and is not stated as an exact identity for a general bounded centered unit-variance X. [Source: PDF page 23, printed page 34; anchor: Remark 2.7.9 displayed expansion.]

Exact standard-normal clause: if X is distributed as N(0,1), then E exp(lambda X) = exp(lambda^2/2) for every lambda in R. [Source: PDF page 13, printed page 24; anchor: equation (2.12), as invoked by Remark 2.7.9 on PDF page 24, printed page 35.]

Exact sub-gaussian characterization clause: for a centered X, Proposition 2.5.2(i)-(iv) are equivalent to the existence of K5 > 0 such that E exp(lambda X) <= exp(K5^2 lambda^2) for every lambda in R; the parameters in the equivalent properties are comparable only up to an absolute constant factor. [Source: PDF page 13, printed page 24; anchor: Proposition 2.5.2(v) and footnote 4.]

Exact sub-exponential characterization clause: for a centered X, Proposition 2.7.1(a)-(d) are equivalent to the existence of K5 > 0 such that E exp(lambda X) <= exp(K5^2 lambda^2) for every lambda satisfying |lambda| <= 1/K5; the parameters in the equivalent properties are comparable only up to an absolute constant factor. [Source: PDF pages 20-21, printed pages 31-32; anchor: Proposition 2.7.1(e) and footnote 7.]

Large-positive-parameter nonintegrability clause: if X is distributed as Exp(1), then E exp(lambda X), viewed as an extended nonnegative expectation, is infinite for every lambda >= 1. Consequently the source says no general all-lambda MGF bound need exist for sub-exponential distributions. [Source: PDF page 24, printed page 35; anchor: last two sentences of Remark 2.7.9.]
definitions_and_conventions: The MGF at lambda is E exp(lambda X); saying it is infinite means the nonnegative expectation diverges rather than giving a finite real value. [Source: PDF page 13, printed page 24, equation (2.12), and PDF page 24, printed page 35, Exp(1) sentence.]
Proposition 2.5.2(i): there is K1 > 0 with P{|X| >= t} <= 2 exp(-t^2/K1^2) for every t >= 0. [Source: PDF page 13, printed page 24; anchor: Proposition 2.5.2(i).]
Proposition 2.5.2(ii): there is K2 > 0 with ||X||_Lp = (E|X|^p)^(1/p) <= K2 sqrt(p) for every p >= 1. [Source: PDF page 13, printed page 24; anchor: Proposition 2.5.2(ii).]
Proposition 2.5.2(iii): there is K3 > 0 with E exp(lambda^2 X^2) <= exp(K3^2 lambda^2) whenever |lambda| <= 1/K3. [Source: PDF page 13, printed page 24; anchor: Proposition 2.5.2(iii).]
Proposition 2.5.2(iv): there is K4 > 0 with E exp(X^2/K4^2) <= 2. [Source: PDF page 13, printed page 24; anchor: Proposition 2.5.2(iv).]
Proposition 2.7.1(a): there is K1 > 0 with P{|X| >= t} <= 2 exp(-t/K1) for every t >= 0. [Source: PDF page 21, printed page 32; anchor: Proposition 2.7.1(a).]
Proposition 2.7.1(b): there is K2 > 0 with ||X||_Lp = (E|X|^p)^(1/p) <= K2 p for every p >= 1. [Source: PDF page 21, printed page 32; anchor: Proposition 2.7.1(b).]
Proposition 2.7.1(c): there is K3 > 0 with E exp(lambda |X|) <= exp(K3 lambda) whenever 0 <= lambda <= 1/K3. [Source: PDF page 21, printed page 32; anchor: Proposition 2.7.1(c).]
Proposition 2.7.1(d): there is K4 > 0 with E exp(|X|/K4) <= 2. [Source: PDF page 21, printed page 32; anchor: Proposition 2.7.1(d).]

The precise constant-comparability convention is that one equivalent property with parameter Ki implies another with parameter Kj <= C Ki for an absolute constant C; numerical equality of the parameters is not claimed. [Source: PDF page 13, printed page 24, footnote 4; PDF page 20, printed page 31, footnote 7.]
For rate r > 0, X distributed as Exp(r) means X is nonnegative and P{X >= t} = exp(-r t) for t >= 0. [Source: PDF page 23, printed page 34; anchor: Example 2.7.8.]

ambiguities.impact: A rigorous asymptotic statement such as E exp(lambda X) = 1 + lambda^2/2 + o(lambda^2) is a natural analyst reconstruction under boundedness, but it is not literally stated with a defined remainder. The contract therefore preserves the source's approximation rather than asserting that reconstruction as an exact source clause.

contract_plain_english: Remark 2.7.9 gives a heuristic, not an exact general formula: for a bounded random variable with mean zero and variance one, its MGF near zero is approximated by the second-order Taylor expression 1 + lambda^2/2, itself approximated by exp(lambda^2/2), as lambda tends to zero (PDF page 23, printed page 34, Remark 2.7.9). Exact equality with exp(lambda^2/2) for every real lambda is asserted only for a standard normal variable (PDF page 13, printed page 24, equation (2.12)). For centered sub-gaussian variables, the exact characterization is existence of some positive K5 giving E exp(lambda X) <= exp(K5^2 lambda^2) for every real lambda, equivalent up to absolute-factor parameter changes to Proposition 2.5.2(i)-(iv) (PDF page 13, printed page 24). For centered sub-exponential variables, the analogous exact characterization holds only when |lambda| <= 1/K5 and is equivalent up to absolute-factor parameter changes to Proposition 2.7.1(a)-(d) (PDF pages 20-21, printed pages 31-32). The restriction to a neighborhood of zero is essential: for the uncentered standard exponential X distributed as Exp(1), the MGF is infinite for every lambda >= 1 (PDF page 24, printed page 35, Remark 2.7.9).
